story: This Hubble Space Telescope image shows the massive elliptical galaxy M60, with part of the faint, bluish spiral galaxy NGC 4647 peeking into the upper right corner. M60 lies about 50 million light-years away inside the Virgo Cluster, an immense gathering of 2,500 galaxies.

An elliptical galaxy is a rounded collection of stars without spiral arms. At its heart M60 holds a monster black hole of 4.5 billion solar masses, which outweighs the Milky Way's central black hole by a factor of more than 1,000.

Close to M60 sits a tiny companion, the ultracompact dwarf galaxy M60-UCD1, which packs 140 million stars into a diameter of about 300 light-years. Using Hubble and the Gemini North telescope, astronomers found that it too holds a supermassive black hole, amounting to 15 percent of its mass. A possible explanation is that M60-UCD1 began as a large galaxy and passed close to the centre of M60 and lost its outer stars and dark matter to it. It may eventually merge with the core of M60.

understand.summary: A composite from Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 cameras. NASA shows F475W and F555W in blue, a blend of F475W, F555W, F850LP and F814W in green, and F850LP and F814W in red.
understand.eye: The colours are hues assigned to several filters, including near-infrared ones that record light the eye cannot see.

explore: M60-UCD1 is the densest galaxy ever seen. Anyone living inside it would see at least 1 million stars with the naked eye, compared with the 4,000 visible from Earth. The finding suggests some dwarf galaxies may be the stripped remains of larger galaxies rather than small star systems that formed on their own.
